catalog_quote: Sri Lanka Portuguese retains the oral vowels of Middle Portuguese (except marginal ə), losing contrastive nasalization, but adding a vowel length contrast, as shown in Table 1. ... Only the last underlying long vowel remains long on the surface, the others being shortened. Stress is non-contrastive, falling on the syllable containing the long vowel, or on the initial syllable if the word has no long vowel (e.g. míída ‘measure’ N, midíí ‘measure’ V, mididóór ‘measurer’, jínjiviri ‘ginger’).

new_statements.quote: p. 67: "Having established the phonemic status of vowel length, we are now in a position to predict stress placement: stress falls on the last underlying long vowel of a word, or on the first vowel of a word having no long vowel." p. 75: "It has been shown that vowel length must be part of the phonological representation of a word and that stress is predictable. We have formulated three rules: a Main Stress Rule, which places stress on the last long vowel of a word, a rule of Length Loss, whereby all unstressed underlying long vowels become surface short vowels, and a scalar rule of Length Adjustment, whereby stressed long vowels in non-initial syllables are reduced in length." new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has a record for Sri Lanka Portuguese with an EMPTY rule field and no existing statements; Smith 1977 supplies the missing placement: weight-sensitive (rightmost heavy = long-vowel syllable, else initial), unbounded, with tertiary stress. This is the primary source every later stress paper on the language cites. Describes the Batticaloa variety (Batticaloa Portuguese, 'BP').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fully predictable from underlying vowel length: main stress falls on the rightmost underlying long vowel of the word; if the word has no long vowel, on the first syllable. Only syllables with long vowels count as heavy. Because unstressed long vowels shorten (Length Loss) and stressed long vowels outside the initial syllable are reduced to half-long, surface length is neutralised outside stressed initial syllables, so the rule is opaque on the surface (stress can surface on initial, antepenultimate, penultimate or final syllables). Domain: the word (lexical categories N, V, etc.); phrase-level Nuclear Stress and Stress Shift rules apply above the word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: pp. 76-78: 'Any word may have an optional tertiary stress preceding its main stress (unless this falls on the first syllable).'.. 'tertiary stress may fall on the second syllable, provided it is closed and that at least one syllable intervenes before the primary stress; otherwise [3stress] falls on the first syllable (provided this is not the position of primary stress).' Tertiary stress immediately before main stress is avoided ('the language appears to be antipathetic towards two succeeding stressed syllables'). At most four stress levels; a phrase-level Nuclear Stress Rule reduces word stresses in syntactic concatenations.
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 18, pp. 67-68: 'Certain clitics and particles are never stressed and presumably must be excluded from the range of L: /ka(n)di/ (intensifier), /fal+a:(#tu)/ (quotative), /ley/ like, /ski/ (attributed speech), /na:/ (tag question), /tu/ (perfective). Others, like /ta:m/ also do get stressed. Still others, like /se:/ (conditional), are optionally stressed.' Case suffixes are stress-neutral, postpositions are not (p. 143ff). Phrase-level Stress Shift (p. 89) moves stress leftwards in some compounds/phrases: 'stress shifts to the second syllable if it is closed, otherwise stress shifts to the first syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress rule sources (Smith 1977, Koontz-Garboden 2000, Seo & Jo 2008) describe Batticaloa (Creole) Portuguese, the Eastern Sri Lanka variety, from Smith's 1973-74 fieldwork. Cardoso's 2015-2020 ELAR deposit covers modern Sri Lanka Portuguese in Ampara, Batticaloa, Jaffna and Trincomalee (Eastern and Northern communities); its orthography marks vowel length by doubling, consistent with the phonemic length on which Smith's rule rests, but the deposit and Cardoso et al. 2019 say nothing about stress placement. The 1811 'grammatical arrangement' in the deposit is Berrenger's grammar of Indo-Portuguese as spoken in India/Ceylon (historical, subscriber access, not opened).

new_statements.quote: p. 1: "According to Smith (1977), stress assignment in Batticaloa Creole Portuguese (BCP) is fully predictable: stress falls on the last underlying long vowel of a word, or on the first short vowel of a word having no long vowel. BCP has phonemic vowel length, although long vowels only surface when they are stressed in a word-initial syllable. Elsewhere, they are shortened." p. 5: "stress is very predictable, but at the same time may occur on any syllable in BCP. In (5)-(8) it occurs in word-initial, antepenultimate, penultimate, and ultimate position." p. 6 fn. 8: "Contrary to Smith's (1977: 71) claim, antepenultimate stress does indeed occur. I thank Smith (p.c.) for providing me with this information and data."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Same rule as Smith 1977, restated in prominence terms: stress the rightmost heavy (long-vowel) syllable, otherwise the leftmost light syllable; not foot-based; only long-vowel syllables are heavy; length is neutralised outside the stressed initial syllable, making the system opaque. Examples: /mi:d/ [mí:d] 'measure', /mi:di:/ [midí] 'to measure', /mi:di:do:r/ [mididór] 'surveyor', /ko:nt/ [kó:nt] 'amount', /disko:nt/ [diskónt] 'discount', /koto:liku/ [kotóliku] 'Catholic', /sindfr/ [síndfr] 'Monday'.

That dissertation was not yet obtained; it is openly available from MPG's Language Description Heritage (CC-BY) and is now saved with a download record at Its section II.3 (pp. 62-100) states the rule explicitly (p. 67: 'stress falls on the last underlying long vowel of a word, or on the first vowel of a word having no long vowel'; p. 63 'Stress.. is fully predictable'), i.e. exactly our classification: weight-sensitive, unbounded, rightmost CVV else initial, non-contrastive.
